analytic.title: A Study of the Impact of Formulation of Cost Function in Task Mapping Problem on NoCs

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Previous works have shown that metaheuristics, such as Genetic Algorithms (GA), are capable of obtaining task mapping solutions in priority-preemptive Network-on-Chip (NoC). However, the solutions obtained with some of these optimization methods do not consider, conjointly, some of the critical characteristics, such as the number of available virtual channels in the routers and memory requirements in the processors. This strategy, in general, renders suboptimal and unsuitable solutions for real platforms. Therefore, we propose the analysis of four objective functions, addressed to unify the end-to-end schedulability analysis considering such platform characteristics. To analyze the objective functions' performance, we conduct a series of experiments mapping the tasks of a benchmark application together with synthetic generated ones onto multiple NoC platforms with realistic characteristics. To compare the proposed cost functions, we use both qualitative and statistical approaches. The results show that the multi-objective formulation is capable of helping the task mapper obtain solutions that are more suitable for real implemented NoC platforms.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Network-on-Chip (NoC) is an acknowledged communication paradigm for on-chip communication that consists of an interconnected fabric that allows data exchange between processor cores of a Multi-processor System-on-Chip (MP-SoC). A Real-time NoC (RTNoC) offers architectural support for the constraints imposed by Real-Time Systems (RTS). It allows real-time guarantees such as Quality-of-Service (QoS) for critical data exchange and greater predictability for the system communication latencies. Our work focuses on the Task Mapping Problem (TMP) in RTNoCs with the following features: (a) wormhole switching strategy that decreases the necessary buffer sizes by dividing the messages transmitted in the network in smaller data units called flits sent in a pipeline fashion through the network; (b) 2D mesh-grid topology due to its simplicity and frequent application in NoC implementations; (c) a deterministic routing algorithm such as the XYrouting that also mitigates deadlock and livelocks from the wormhole switching; (d) Virtual Channels (VC) that increase the NoC throughput and allow message preemption; (e) an amount of required local memory for the processor cores.

VCs are dedicated buffers placed at routers' inputs that allow priority-preemption when multiple messages compete. VCs enable passage for the flits from messages with higher priority while storing inside of its buffers the flits from those messages of lower-priority until the moment that the lower priority message is enabled passage after all higher-priority messages are transmitted. For message priority-preemption functionality to work, it is required for the NoC to have prioritized VCs with separated service levels. However, the system would require a VC buffer per task in the mapped Real-Time Application (RTA), as shown in [1]. This approach requires a prohibitive number of VCs in the system. Thankfully, the work present in [2] shows that the number of necessary VCs in the routers' inputs should be equal to the number of message contentions in the network.

It is also essential to ensure that the amount of memory required by each core must not exceed the amount of memory available. This restriction relies on the hardware architecture of the MPSoC, and task scheduling techniques that do not take this into account can lead to unrealistic solutions [3]. This makes clear the benefit of having techniques that, besides guaranteeing allocation of tasks (present in the RTA) onto the processor cores, also allow to minimize the amount of memory required in the processors.

The Task Mapping Problem (TMP) is expressed as the allocation of tasks present in the RTA onto the multiple processor cores. TMP is an N P -complete problem in which given an RTA composed of n tasks to be mapped onto the m processor cores of an NoC platform, and reflecting in a design space of m n possible task mapping solutions [4]. This large amount of possible solutions makes a naive brute-force approach impossible. Looking for better results in the optimization processes, researchers usually test new metaheuristics to compare their results. However, the optimization processes are very sensitive to the way the cost function is formulated. Although our study focuses on homogeneous NoC-Based MPSoCs, their results have generated a better understanding of how the formulation of cost functions impact the optimization processes in the specific case of TMP.

In this perspective, the contributions of this work are: (i) the study of the behavior of four objective functions used to guide the optimization process of four different metaheuristics, (ii) the evaluation of both Single-Objective and Multi-Objective Optimization (resp., SOO, and MOO) aspects as strategies to be addressed for the TMP, (iii) the evaluation of these objective functions using non-parametric statistical significance tests, and (iv) the analysis of the impact of the formulation of the cost function in TMP by using a metaheuristic independent perspective, which for the best of our acknowledge is a novel feature. To do that, we have collected all the results from the four metaheuristics used over a set RTAs, and focusing the statistical tests on evaluating the performance of the proposed four cost functions.

The timing aspects of these objective functions use the schedulability analysis given in [5]. To do that our approach considers three aspects (metrics) to build suitable cost functions: the number (a) of unscheduled tasks, and (b) of virtual channels, and (c) the required memory as proposed in [3].

div.head: II. RELATED WORKS
div.p: Metaheuristics to optimize the TMP for NoCs have been applied in several works using mainly Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [6], and Genetic Algorithm (GA) [7] [8]. Such methods are capable of obtaining fully schedulable task mapping solutions. Since PSO and GA are search-based evolutionary optimization methods, they require an objective function to evaluate through their iterations and point them to better solutions that, in turn, reflect solutions with better metrics values, which is important for the system functionality. Previous works have applied objective functions focused in (a) timing requirements [7] [8], (b) energy dissipation [9], and (c) required local memory in processor cores [3].

To the best of our knowledge, the only work that targets the number of required virtual channels to be minimized is [2]. Regarding the current work, [2] presents a more complex approach using a three stage optimization process through a Simulated Annealing heuristic: The first stage maps tasks with heavy communication adjacently, the second minimizes the number of required VCs per router, and the third one optimizes the timing requirements using the size of the messages. Meanwhile, our approach takes advantage of a single optimization stage, using one of the proposed objective functions, including both SOO and MOO as optimization strategies. In this manner, it is possible to take into consideration simultaneously multiple system characteristics such as timing requirements, number of VCs, and memory consumption. div.head: III. TASK MAPPING AS AN OPTIMIZATION PROBLEM
A. System Model
div.p: In our work the NoC platform Ψ is modeled as a set of m homogeneous processor cores placed in tiles with local memories and network interface modules Π = {π 0 , ..., π m-1 }. Each tile has a local memory responsible for storing code memory from the tasks mapped to that processor core and the messages that these tasks may emit and receive. These tiles are then connected to a set of m routers R = {ρ 0 , ..., ρ m-1 } with these components displaced in a meshgrid topology and connected by a set of unidirectional links Λ = {λ π0,ρ0 , λ ρ0,π0 , λ ρ0,ρ1 , ...}. In our study, we assume a system with homogeneous processors, and each processor core has the same amount of private local memory memcap(π) in bytes. Other NoC characteristics are: (a) λ wd representing the links width in bits, (b) L ρ the latency to route and transmit a header flit in cycles, and (c) L λ is latency to transmit a flit. Figure 1 shows a representation of a modeled RTNoC composed of 9 processor cores placed in a 3 × 3 mesh-grid where red circles represent the processors connected to their respective network-interface modules, blue squares represent routers, and green squares are tiles that contain these elements. Each router ρ i ∈ R has a set of input and output unidirectional links that compose, respectively, the sets inputl(ρ i ) and outputl(ρ i ).

The number of links in these sets depends on the position of the router, for example, inputl(ρ 0 ) = {λ π0,ρ0 , λ ρ1,ρ0 , λ ρ3,ρ0 }. A router ρ i has for each input link a set of VCs expressed as vc(ρ i ) and each VC buffer has a capacity to store a certain amount of flits represented as buf f vc(ρ i ). Since the NoC is homogeneous, every router has the same number of VCs per link, so to represent this fact, we define it as vc(Ψ).

div.head: B. Application Model
div.p: The RTA Ω is represented as a set of n periodic tasks Γ = {τ 0 , ..., τ n-1 } where the ith task is represented as a tuple τ i = C i , T i , D i , P i , R i , M i , φ i that is composed by the following elements: (a) C i is the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), (b) T i is the task inter-arrival period, (c) D i is the deadline, (d) P i is the task priority-level, (e) R i is the Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) that depends on the mapping, (f) M i is the required code memory to execute the task in bytes, and (g) φ i is a packetized message sent after the task execution to another task in Γ as a flow of flits. Note that if the task τ i does not send any message then φ i = ∅.

The ith message in Φ is expressed as a tuple φ i = τ di , L i , Z i , K i , S i where (a) τ di is the message's destination task, (b) L i is the basic transmission latency that depends on the mapping, (c) Z i is the size of the message in bytes, (d) K i is the maximum release jitter to start transmit the message, and (e) S i is the message Worst-Case Latency Time (WCLT) that also depends on the mapping. Note that in the worst-case scenario, the maximum jitter suffered by a message is equal to the WCRT from its source task

In our case, we define the following functions to aid notation for the objective function definitions: (a) index returns the index of a processor core; (b) map returns the processor π m that a task τ n is mapped to; (c) map -1 returns the set of tasks mapped to a processor cores; (d) route returns the set of links that forms a path in which a message φ i transverse from its source task τ i to its destination τ di ; (e) route -1 returns the set of messages that transverses a link λ i ; (f) cont d returns a set of higher priority messages that directly interfere with a message φ i ; (g) cont d i returns a set of higher priority message that downstream indirectly interfere with a message φ i . The concepts of direct and indirect interference for message priority-preemption are given in [5].

For each task τ i , its WCRT is calculated using the recursive response time analysis in Eq. 1. Meanwhile, a message φ i has its WCLT calculated using the method present in [5] that also uses a recursive method, as shown in Eq. 2.

div.p: At last, we assess whether the ith task is schedulable in an end-to-end sense by checking if its WCRT and its message's WCLT is smaller or equal than its deadline. In other words, if R i + S i ≤ D i then the task τ i is schedulable. An RTA Ω is fully schedulable if all of its tasks are themselves schedulable. Since the schedulability of an RTA strongly depends on the task mapping, we define a function in Eq. 6 that returns all non-schedulable tasks given a task mapping x, the RTA, and the platform Ψ, in which it will be mapped onto.
div.formula: unsch(x, Ω, Ψ) = {τ i ∈ Γ : R i + S i > D i }.(6)
div.p: Another aspect that depends on the task mapping that can be measured is the maximum required local memory per tile, as proposed in [3]. The amount of required local memory for a processor core π i is calculated using the following equation:
div.formula: reqmem(x, π i ) = ∀τ j ∈map -1 (π i ) M j + ∀φ j ∈sendby(π i ) Z j + ∀φ j ∈sendto(π i ) Z j ,(7)
div.p: where sendby(π i ) = route -1 (λ πi,ρi ) is a set of messages transmitted from a processor core π i , sendto(π i ) = route -1 (λ ρi,πi ) is a set of messages transmitted to a processor core π i , and x is a task mapping solution.

Since the system is homogeneous, the required amount of local memory per tile (sreqmem) equals the maximum required amount of memory necessary to correctly execute the RTA without overloading any of the system's local memories, as given in Eq. 8:

Otherwise, the required number of VCs in the router should be equal to the number of message contentions in each router to avoid buffering effects that are not covered in the real-time model present, and, therefore, not upper-bounded. For this reason, we need to first formulate an expression to identify the amount of message contention per router. Each router ρ i contains a set of output links outputl(ρ i ), and by identifying the maximum number of messages that transverse each of these links λ ∈ outputl(ρ i ), we identify the required number of virtual channels during the worst-case scenario where all messages are under conflict. We select the output links because, in the scenario of multiple message preemption, the blocked messages will be stored in the buffers in VCs in the input ports. This number can be expressed as a function vcreq that is calculated using Eq. 9.
div.formula: vcreq(x, Ω, Ψ) = max ∀ρ∈R max ∀λ∈outputl(ρ i ) |route -1 (λ)| . (9)

div.head: IV. FOUR OBJECTIVE FUNCTIONS
div.p: To carry out a comparative study, we will introduce 4 cost functions. The first one will assess the number of unscheduled tasks within an application, considering their deadlines, priorities, and the latency of the messages sent. This cost function represents a Single-Objective Optimization (SOO) approach, which will allow us to compare the other 3 cost functions that focus on a Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) approach. Our method focuses on evaluating examples based on the system and application models proposed in Section III.

div.head: A. SOO
div.p: The first objective function, f EERT in Eq. 10, is used in a Single-Objective Optimization as a single numeric value metric. It returns the number of non-schedulable tasks focusing only on timing requirements. Previous works focus only on such objective functions and take into consideration only the real-time characteristics of the task mapping.

div.head: B. MOO by Weighted Sum Objective Rating Optimizations
div.p: The second and third objective functions in Eqs. 11 and 12 resp., follow a Multi-Objective Optimization approach that uses a single linear function weighted by a sum of different metrics (partial cost-functions), in which each metric provides a positive scalar weight that is then aggregated to a single value. Some drawbacks of this approach discussed in [10] limit its usage when treating with conflicting or mutually dependent cost-functions. Despite this, this method is used in this work because we actually sought a method that gives different levels of importance to the different objectives.
div.formula: fCCEERT (x, Ω, Ψ) =wvc (max (vcreq(x) -vc(Ψ), 0)) + fEERT (x, Ω, Ψ),(11)
div.p: where w vc and w eert are the weighting values that define the importance and inter-relationship between the number of VCs and the number of non-schedulable tasks. Since it is important to require fewer VCs than the number available, w vc is defined to be greater than the maximum value of f EERT . Knowing that the maximum number of non-schedulable tasks is the number of tasks in the real-time application |Γ|, then we set w vc = 10|Γ|. In this manner, the objective function receives a strong penalty when the mapping requires a larger number of VCs than the available and while still evaluating the number of non-schedulable tasks.
fccmemeert(x, Ω, Ψ) =wvc (max (vcreq(x) -vc(Ψ), 0)) + weert fEERT (x)+ wmem sreqmem(x),

where both w eert and w vc are as in Eq. 11, and w mem is obtained using Eq. 13. The chosen value of w mem normalizes the memory term of the objective and uses it to differentiate between task mapping solutions that have the same values of non-schedulable tasks by their memory usage while giving a smaller rating for this metric when compared to the other two.
wmem = 1

div.head: C. MOO using Pareto Front
div.p: The Multi-Objective Optimization based in Pareto Front merges multiple metrics in a vector of objective functions that may conflict with each other, characterizing a non-linear problem in the space of objectives. An important concept to measure the quality of solutions in MOO is the notion of dominance, as defined in [11]. However, as a consequence of the dominance concept, the optimization process yields a set of solutions where none of them dominate each other, known as the non-dominated set. A set of solutions obtained is named Pareto Front (PF), which is a curve in the space of objective functions, where all elements are non-dominated.
The fourth objective function, F M OO in Eq. 14, follows a MOO Pareto front approach with metrics for (a) timing requirements, (b) number of VCs, and (c) required memory:
div.formula: F M OO (x, Ψ, Ω) = {f EERT (x), sreqmem(x), vcreq(x)}. (14
div.p: The function F M OO targets all metrics with the same level of importance allowing the designer to pick the Pareto optimal solutions that he/she judges to be suitable. However, depending on the system design, these metrics have an innate level of dependency. For example, if a system does not have all of its tasks schedulable, the system is not suitable for a hard-/firm-real-time setting, but it is still usable as a soft real-time one, which accepts a deterioration in performance.

Meanwhile, the required local memory depends on how large the required value is. If the value is not prohibitive, it is negotiable, and with a higher cost, larger memories are feasible. The same applies to a different design cost for the number of VCs: if it is too large the task mapping solution would not be feasible.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
div.p: The proposed experimental setup applies the objective functions: (1) f EERT (Eq. 10), (2) f CCEERT (Eq. 11), (3) f CCM EM EERT (Eq. 12), and (4) F M OO .

An extensive range of settings was used, varying the use of (a) metaheuristics, (b) real-time applications and (c) NoC platform characteristics. The experiment goal is to observe a possible inner-relationship between the three metrics (nonschedulable tasks, required number of VCs, and required local memory), when using our four proposed objective functions.

The experiments setup use three NoC platforms configurations: (a) Config1, and (b) Config2, and (c) Synth. These configurations vary the platform route and link latencies L ρ and L λ . The first two are based on implemented NoC platforms, while the SynthNoC is a synthetic configuration with unrealistic long link latencies to experiment on timing constraints. For each configuration, five topology sizes were used giving 15 different NoC configurations. See Table I.

For the RTAs, the benchmark application is called Autonomous Vehicle Application (AVA) [12] together with four synthetic random-generated applications: Normal, Normal1, Uniform, and Uniform1. The synthetic applications were generated using random normal and uniform distributions for their tasks periods, varying in [0.05, 1] s, utilization factors ranging in [1, 75] %, messages sizes varying in [128, 65536] bytes, and tasks code memory in [2048,16384] bytes. The utilization factor is the fraction of the time that a processor spends executing a task. Each of these RTA characteristics is present in Table II, where U represents the utilization factor, Z the message size, and M the code memory for a task. Since a TMP is the mapping of an RTA onto an NoC platform, our experiment tests 75 different TMPs from combining three NoC platforms, five mesh-grid sizes, and five RTAs. Ultimately, we analyze the objective functions using the 75 TMPs under four different task mappers that uses metaheuristic algorithms present in related works, namely: (a) GA [7], (b) an adaptive version of GA (AGA) [6], (c) a discrete PSO (DPSO) [8], and (d) a Multi-Objective GA (NSGAII) [13] when using F M OO cost function. The parameters for these metaheuristics are present in Table III. Since NSGA-II is a multi-objective optimizer, its result is a Pareto set of solutions. To compare with the other results, we only used the best solution for each individual metric from its Pareto set of solutions.

div.head: A. Graphical Analysis
div.p: To illustrate the experimental results obtained using the four proposed objective functions, we took the median of the 50 results of task mappers using each one of the metaheuristics (GA [7] , AGA [8], DPSO [6], and NSGA-II [13]) using each of the four objective functions. We then took the average for the results of the single-objective functions, namely, f EERT , f CCEERT , and f CCM EM EERT , executed by the metaheuristics (GA, AGA, and DPSO). Meanwhile, since F M OO was only executed using NSGA-II, its median value stays the same.

We have done so to compare the overall quality of results for all four objective functions in a metaheuristic independent perspective. These median values were plot in multiple graphs when mapping one RTA (AVA) onto various platforms with different sizes using the configurations Config1 and Synth. The reasoning for the choice for this particular sub-set of results is that we can observe the behavior of the objective functions when dealing with this well-known application (AVA).

Figure 2 shows the results for three metrics when mapping AVA onto different platforms using Config1 setting. The three metrics presented are: (a) the number of non-schedulable tasks representing the timing requirements, (b) the number of required VCs, and (c) the required local memory size in KB. Figure 3 shows the same application (AVA) when mapped to platforms using Synth setting. By comparing the figures visually, it is possible to observe that by changing the platforms, there is not much difference in the results obtained with the different objective functions, save some fluctuation due to the random nature of the metaheuristics used. The only metric that seems to have a consistent difference in results when changing the platforms is the number of non-schedulable tasks metric. In this metric, the platforms' characteristics influence the messages WCLT value (as shown in Eq. 2 and Eq. 3).

Overall in Figs. 2a and 3a it is possible to observe that, as expected, as the number of available processor cores increases, the task mappers obtain more solutions with less nonschedulable tasks and even fully schedulable solutions. One compelling examination is that f CCEERT and f CCM EM EERT obtain solutions that require fewer VCs than the other objective functions and, in the majority of times, the number of needed VCs is the same amount of VCs available in the NoC platforms. It means that, for these cases, the task mapping solutions require less effort to be directly used by a designer in an NoC platform. F M OO does not yield solutions with the same amount of required VCs. It may be because the evolutionary pressure from F M OO , where all three metrics have the same weight, are not strong enough to concentrate the search in regions of the design space that require less VCs.

Another examination is that, in these observed cases, f CCM EM EERT were capable of obtaining better or similar required local memory results than F M OO . It may indicate that with a higher pressure to find solutions that need fewer VCs, therefore contains fewer message conflicts, the tasks are mapped in a more spread fashion, and it, in turn, reduces the required local memory per tile.

div.head: B. Statistical Analysis over the 4 cost functions
div.p: It is possible to use all gathered data as samples for a statistical analysis to identify whether there are significant differences between these objective functions, using all the experiment executed over the 75 different TMPs. First, we group the results that uses the same TMP, i.e. mapping a RTA to a particular NoC, and rank the median of the results of optimization using all four objective function depending on a metric. For example, in Fig. 2c, when mapping AVA onto a Config1 2 × 2 NoC, we can infer that f CCM EM EERT has the minimal value and rank 1, F M OO has the second best value and rank 2, and so on. We then take all the average for these rankings for each objective function to observe which one of them is more suitable for each metric. These averages are present in Table V. We can observe that, as expected, f EERT has the best ranking regarding the number of non-schedulable tasks. However, since it only checks this characteristic, it has the worst rankings regarding the number of required VCs and local memory per tile.

We then use a Friedman statistic with the null-hypothesis that all objective functions have statistically the same results for each metric. We obtain for all three the following Friedman statistics of 29.68, 370.12, and 520.70, respectively for the non-schedulable tasks, number of VCs and memory metrics. All three related p-values for these statistics are below that 0.05 threshold, rejecting the null hypothesis with a α = 5% significance that the objective functions results are the same for the chosen metrics. We then proceed to use a post-hoc method to compare pair-wise the objective functions for each metric. Using a significance level α = 0.05 we can observe in Table IV that F M OO and f EERT are statistically the same regarding the number of non-schedulable tasks. The same is true for the pair f CCEERT and f CCM EM EERT . This is a strong claim for f CCM EM EERT , since it suggest that it have similar results regarding the timing constraints while taking into consideration the required memory. Also, for required VCs, we observe that f CCEERT and f M EM CCEERT are statistically equal. The same happens for F M OO and f CCEERT observing the adjusted p-value. It means that the results f CCM EM EERT are significantly different than the other metrics that observe the number of VCs required by the mapping. At last, for required memory, we observe that only the pair F M OO and f CCM EM EERT are not significantly different. It means that their results can be interchangeable regarding the required local memory.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: Four objective functions (using three different metrics) were proposed that aid the designer to obtain task mappings with a near-optimal number of non-schedulable tasks, using the proposed models; and reducing the required memory with virtual channels close to the amount available to the NoC platform. We added a formulation into the wormhole-based NoC platform to define these objective functions, considering extended models for both the system and the application. Our results were achieved by an experimental analysis using a lot of experiments, obtaining competitive results.
